# Draft:Biases in Jury Decision-Making__disambig_2

Juror Bias
Juror bias refers to the ways in which a jurors' decisions may be influenced by characteristics such as age, race, or gender. These biases can affect verdicts, sentencing, and the evaluation of witnesses, attorneys, and defendants. Research on juror biases includes both real-world court data and mock-jury studies that simulate trials to examine how these factors influence juror decision-making.
General Overview
The role of a juror is to listen to the evidence presented in trial, evaluate the facts, and make an impartial decision regarding whether the defendant is guilty in a criminal case or liable in a civil case. Jurors are instructed to be impartial. However, implicit biases, which are unconscious predispositions that can automatically influence perceptions and interactions, may affect their decisions. Unlike explicit bias, which involves conscious beliefs or prejudices, implicit bias operates without awareness and can shape snap judgments during trials. Implicit biases can impact verdicts, sentencing decisions, and the perceived fairness of a trial.
Methods and Measurements
Biases in jury decision-making are typically studied using mock jury designs, in which participants are asked to act as jurors in a simulated trial. Mock-jury studies are used because they allow researchers to isolate specific factors while maintaining experimental control. Participants may read, listen to, or watch trial materials, often based on real-world trials but altered to be less recognizable. After being exposed to the trial information, mock jurors complete questionnaires assessing their verdicts, confidence in their verdicts, sentencing recommendations, and perceptions of credibility for the people involved in the trial. Some research also includes a deliberation aspect in which jurors provide individual verdicts, deliberate with a group of other jurors, and provide a post-deliberation verdict.
To study biases in the jury decision-making process, researchers manipulate the characteristics of the people in the trial stimuli. For instance, the age, race, or gender of the defendant, witness, or attorney could be manipulated through written description, using photographs, or by using videos.
Age Biases
Defendants
U.S. federal court data indicate that jurors and judges tend to be more lenient towards older defendants (60+ years old), with younger defendants (under 60 years old) more likely to be incarcerated.. Meta-analytic research, which statistically combines results from multiple studies, indicates that defendant age does not affect sentence length .
Mock-jury research found that there was leniency towards both older and younger defendants depending on the type of crime presented. For murder cases, mock jurors assigned longer sentences to the 40-year-old defendant versus the 20 and 60-year-old defendants, and no age differences were found when the defendant was accused of theft. .
Witnesses
Age-related perceptions similarly extend to witnesses, influencing their credibility in the eyes of jurors. Research on eyewitnesses finds that child (vs. adult) witnesses are generally seen as less credible when testifying in court . An additional study found that a child witness led to fewer guilty verdicts than an adult witness . Children under 10 years old were perceived as having poorer recall than children over 12 years old, and witnesses under the age of 18 were seen as more credible when they provide smooth testimony with little hesitation .
Attorneys
Research the effect of attorney age on jurors' decisions is limited.
Racial Biases
Defendants
Meta-analytic findings concluded that there was a small effect of defendant race on verdicts and sentencing decisions, resulting in harsher judgements for defendants of another race than the jurors' own . This bias was particularly pronounced among Black participants and in samples from the general population compared with university student samples.
Meta-analytic findings showed that mock jurors did not treat defendants differently based on their race except for in drug crimes, which were associated with a small racial bias effect against both Black and Latino (vs. White) defendants . An additional meta-analysis indicated finding no significant effect of race on legal decisions made by practitioners, investigators, and mock juries in cases involving forensic evidence .
A literature review concluded that jurors made harsher decisions when: (a) the defendant was of a different race than them and (b) when the defendant and victim were of different races . Differences were specifically observed when defendant race was made salient in the stimuli. For instance, White mock jurors failed to show racial biases, and Black mock jurors showed leniency towards defendants of their own racial group .
Racially diverse (vs. all-White) juries increased jurors’ cognitive depletion but also increased the number of case facts jurors discussed during deliberation when the defendant was Black . Regardless of deliberation, mock jurors were less likely to convict the Black (vs. White) defendants.
When the death penalty was possible, mock jurors had an 80% conviction rate for Black defendants and a 55.1% conviction rate for White defendants . Research using photos of real defendants facing the possibility of the death penalty in Philadelphia found that defendants who were rated as being more stereotypically Black were more likely to be sentenced to death (vs. life in prison) .
U.S. federal court data show that Hispanic defendants were more likely to be incarcerated than defendants of other races, with both Black and Hispanic defendants receiving the longest sentences compared with White defendants .
Witnesses
For eyewitnesses, race generally does not affect verdicts. However, in a murder trial with a Black defendant, Black eyewitnesses were rated as more credible then White eyewitnesses . For character witnesses, the race of the witness did not affect mock jurors’ verdicts . The race (Black vs. White) of a co-conspirator informant witness did not affect mock jurors’ verdicts in a drug case .
Attorneys
Mock jurors perceived Mexican American defense attorneys as less competent when representing Mexican American (vs. European American) defendants, though the attorney race did not affect verdicts . Black attorneys were associated with higher likelihood of guilty verdicts in murder trials . A literature review suggested a potential interaction between attorney and defendant race called for more research on this topic .
Gender Biases
Defendants
Data from the U.S. Department of Justice show a 565% increase in the rate of incarcerated women between 1980 and 2022 . Men are about 74% more likely to be incarcerated than women for similar offenses .
In cases of intimate partner violence, female defendants with male victims were treated more leniently than male defendants with female victims . A meta-analysis of mock jury studies confirmed that women generally receive shorter sentences than men across crime types . This pattern is thought to reflect cultural stereotypes linking masculinity with criminality  and associate men with more aggressive attitudes .
Witnesses
Female expert witnesses are perceived as more credible in fields dominated by women, and male experts were perceived as more credible in fields dominated by men . Gender effects also interact with testimony complexity, with male experts being rated as more persuasive when testimony is complex and female experts being more persuasive when testimony is simple . When perceived as less likeable or knowledgeable, female experts were rated more negatively than male experts . A literature review revealed that expert witness gender influenced the overall trial outcomes in civil cases but has little effect on outcomes in criminal cases .
Attorneys
Mock jurors were more likely to acquit defendants represented by male (vs. female) attorneys and showed a preference for attorneys who shared their own gender . Male attorneys expressing anger in court were viewed more positively than female attorneys expressing anger . Mock jurors used anger as a reason to hire male attorneys and to avoid hiring female attorneys. In a mock trial involving alleged rape, mock jurors rated a female (vs. male) prosecuting attorney as less competent and a female (vs. male) defense attorney as more competent. These perceptions of attorney competence, in turn, influenced jurors’ verdicts .
Intersectionality
Intersectionality is the idea that a person's social identities, such as race, gender, and age combine to shape their experiences and the advantages and disadvantages they face . This framework emphasizes that social categories such as race and gender do not operate independently but interact to create complex patterns of disadvantage in contexts such as criminal sentencing. In archival research on defendant race, gender, and age in Wisconsin, Black male defendants were the most likely to receive jail sentences, whereas Black female defendants were the least likely to receive jail sentences . In the same data, younger defendants generally had lower odds of incarceration, with the exception of Black male defendants, who were more likely to be incarcerated.
Archival research in Pennsylvania revealed that young Black male and Hispanic male defendants received longer sentences than any other intersectional identities in the sample, and the shortest sentences were assigned to older defendants and young female defendants . Archival research using U.S. federal court data showed a similar pattern, finding that younger Hispanic male defendants were the most likely to be incarcerated, whereas young Black male defendants were the most likely to receive longer sentences .
Overall, research suggests that jurors' decisions are influenced by multiple social characteristics, and ongoing research continues to examine how theses biases shape legal decisions across different courtroom roles.
